# Audience heatmap

Status: chosen, 7 November 2026.

## Idea

A startup fills in the same short form as the [ad channel mispricing finder](ad-channel-mispricing.md): industry, the startup in one sentence, the target customer in one sentence, what a customer pays, monthly advertising budget, and markets. It gets back a heatmap of a city showing where its target customers live, work and pass through, where competitors already advertise to them, and the gap between the two. The run ends with specific placements to buy in the strongest gap areas. The demo city is New York.

It is for startups that want customers beyond Meta and Google but have no media agency and a limited budget.

## Origin

Raised by Viktor on 7 November 2026 as a pivot from the ad channel mispricing finder. That idea needed prices for advertising placements, which are mostly unpublished, while public data about where people live, work and travel is plentiful. The competition and gap layers, the competitor-campaign agent and the closing list of placements were suggested by an agent in the same conversation, and the user accepted them.

## How it works

Decided on 7 November 2026; the decisions are in [product.md](../product.md).

1. Input: the onboarding form above. The target customer sentence becomes filters on census and trip data, such as age, income, industry and household type.
2. Audience fit layer: each area of the city is scored by how many target customers live there, work there or pass through it.
3. Competition layer: a browser agent finds the startup's competitors, then searches press, trade sites and social media for their outdoor campaigns in the city, such as "<competitor> subway ad" or "<competitor> billboard NYC", and places each find on the map. Where it finds nothing, competitors' stores and offices stand in.
4. Gap layer: areas with high audience fit and low competition. This is the default view; the other two layers are toggles that explain it.
5. Placements: specific placements a startup can buy inside the strongest gap areas, such as LinkNYC kiosks and bus shelters, each with an estimated cost per audience member and a way to measure it (a QR code, promo code or landing page). Budget filters out placements with minimum spends.

An hourly view of the audience fit layer, using subway and taxi data by hour, is an open option, not a decision.

## Evidence and data

Checked on 7 November 2026 by querying each source's API or download index. "Checked" means we fetched the column list, a sample row and the row count or file list; no full download has been run. The New York open data portals (data.cityofnewyork.us and data.ny.gov) list no licence on these datasets.

Who lives where:

- US Census Bureau American Community Survey, 5-year estimates for 2024 (fetched): `tools.census` writes `data/census/nyc_tracts.csv`, one row for each of New York City's 2,327 census tracts (an area of about 4,000 people). Columns: population, median age, median household income, per capita income, and the shares aged 20 to 34, with a bachelor's degree or higher (of those aged 25 and over), with household income of $150,000 or more, and enrolled in college. Median household income is missing for 128 tracts and is capped at $250,001 by the Census Bureau. The API needs a key, read from `CENSUS_API_KEY` in `tools/.env`. Tract boundaries for the map are not fetched yet.

Who works where:

- US Census Bureau [LODES](https://lehd.ces.census.gov/data/lodes/LODES8/ny/) (job counts by home and work location), version 8: files for New York State run to 2024. Workplace files count jobs per census block by earnings band and industry, and origin-destination files link home and work blocks. They show daytime audiences, such as finance workers in Midtown.

Who passes through:

- [MTA Subway Hourly Ridership: Beginning 2025](https://data.ny.gov/d/5wq4-mkjj) (checked): 47.4 million rows, updated 4 November 2026. Each row is one station complex, one hour and one fare class, with ridership, transfers, latitude and longitude. The fare class category, such as full fare or student, gives a rough audience signal. Earlier years are in separate datasets (2017 to 2019, and 2020 to 2024).
- [Pickups and Drop-offs by Taxi Zone and Industry](https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/c5iv-bn4s) (checked): monthly counts per taxi zone for yellow taxis, green taxis and high-volume ride-hail companies, with data to September 2026. [Taxi zone shapes](https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/8meu-9t5y) are a separate dataset.
- TLC [trip record files](https://www.nyc.gov/site/tlc/about/tlc-trip-record-data.page) (file list checked): monthly Parquet files to September 2026 for yellow taxis and high-volume ride-hail. Fares and tips per trip could serve as a rough income signal; the columns were not checked.
- [Citi Bike trip data](https://s3.amazonaws.com/tripdata/index.html) (file list checked): monthly files to October 2026, under Citi Bike's [data sharing policy](https://www.citibikenyc.com/data-sharing-policy), which was not read.
- [Bi-Annual Pedestrian Counts](https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/cqsj-cfgu) (checked): only 114 locations, mostly retail corridors and bridges, counted in May and September or October for morning, midday and evening, from 2007 to May 2026. Too sparse for a citywide layer; useful to check the other layers at those points.

Where ads can be bought:

- [LinkNYC Kiosk Locations](https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/s4kf-3yrf) (checked): 2,255 sites with address, coordinates and census tract. By kiosk type: 2,032 live Link1.0 kiosks, 151 live Link5G kiosks marked "Ad", 57 live Link5G kiosks marked "NonAd", and a few removed or payphones. Only the Link5G types say whether they carry ads; whether Link1.0 kiosks do is unchecked.
- [Bus Stop Shelters](https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/t4f2-8md7) (checked): 3,312 shelters with coordinates and neighbourhood, updated 1 October 2026. The data has no field saying whether a shelter carries advertising.
- [DOB Sign Application Filings](https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/nyis-y4yr) (checked): 15,288 filings, but only from April 2013 to October 2017. It covers all signs, not only advertising, and gives an address and tax lot rather than coordinates. Not usable as a current billboard map.

Competitors:

- Competitors' outdoor campaigns: no public list exists, so the agent in step 3 gathers them from press, trade sites and social media.
- Competitors' stores and offices: OpenStreetMap or a places API. Not checked.

## Existing products

No search has been run yet. From memory: foot-traffic and audience-mapping products such as Placer.ai already map where audiences go, and AdQuick offers audience modelling for outdoor advertising. The audience heatmap differs by mapping one startup's customer from a one-sentence description, adding a layer of competitors' actual outdoor campaigns, and ending with placements to buy. Without the competition layer it would be close to products that already exist.

## Tracks it could serve

- G-Research: strong. The hidden things are where a startup's customers are and where competitors haven't reached them. They are found by combining public datasets with an agent's search for campaigns, and they tell the startup where to advertise, which covers the brief's three questions.
- HRT: moderate. Stronger with the hourly view, which would forecast when an area holds the most target customers and turn that into a buying decision.
- Wordsmith: moderate. The competitor-campaign agent is a multi-step browser workflow: find competitors, search several kinds of site, read the results and place each campaign. The rest of the product is data processing, not browser work.
- Bank of Scotland: weak. It serves startups, not consumers' cost of living.
- Metaview overall prize: a city heatmap is a strong visual demo.

## Challenges it could use

- Gemini API: the competitor-campaign agent and turning the target customer sentence into data filters.
- Tiger Data: hourly ridership and trip data are time series, which fits the hourly view if it is built.
- Vultr: hosting the data processing or the demo.

## Open problems

- Licences: the New York open data portals list none on the datasets checked, and Citi Bike's data sharing policy has not been read.
- Billboards have no current public map. The only sign dataset stops in 2017, so the placements step relies on LinkNYC kiosks and bus shelters, and on shelters only if we can find which ones carry advertising.
- The competitor-campaign agent may find few campaigns for small competitors, leaving the competition layer mostly made of stores and offices, which show where competitors are, not where they advertise.
- Turning a one-sentence target customer into census and trip filters is untested, and some customers, such as "developers at Series A startups", have no direct census field.
- Prices for LinkNYC kiosks and bus shelters are probably unpublished, so cost per audience member would be an estimate. How to estimate it is undecided.
- Judges in Edinburgh may ask why New York. The answer is that New York publishes the most data and the method works elsewhere, which the pitch should say up front.
- The mispricing claim of the earlier idea, and the Revolut evidence behind it, no longer support the product directly. The pitch needs its own evidence that competitors leave gaps in a city.

## Scope

New York only, with its data gathered ahead of time by scripts in `tools/`. Demo one startup end to end: the form, the gap map with the audience fit and competition layers as toggles, the competitor campaigns the agent found, and the placements to buy in the top gap areas. A recorded run of the competitor agent is kept as a fallback in case the live agent fails.

## Alternatives

- [Ad channel mispricing finder](ad-channel-mispricing.md): the idea this replaces. It ranked specific placements, last narrowed to airports, by cost per attentive second weighted by audience value, but most placement prices are unpublished. It shares the onboarding form and the aim of reaching customers competitors miss.

"""Fetch American Community Survey data for every census tract in New York City.

Reads CENSUS_API_KEY from tools/.env or the environment. Writes the raw API
responses to data/raw/census/ and one row per tract to data/census/nyc_tracts.csv.
"""

import csv
import json
import os
import time
import urllib.error
import urllib.parse
import urllib.request
from pathlib import Path

YEAR = "2024"
DATASET = f"https://api.census.gov/data/{YEAR}/acs/acs5"
STATE = "36"
# Bronx, Brooklyn (Kings), Manhattan (New York), Queens, Staten Island (Richmond).
COUNTIES = {
    "005": "Bronx",
    "047": "Brooklyn",
    "061": "Manhattan",
    "081": "Queens",
    "085": "Staten Island",
}

# Age 20 to 34: male rows 8 to 12 and female rows 32 to 36 of table B01001.
AGE_20_34 = [f"B01001_{n:03d}E" for n in [*range(8, 13), *range(32, 37)]]
# Bachelor's, master's, professional and doctorate degrees, of people aged 25+.
DEGREE = [f"B15003_{n:03d}E" for n in range(22, 26)]
# Household income of $150,000 or more.
INCOME_150K = ["B19001_016E", "B19001_017E"]
# Enrolled in college as an undergraduate or graduate student.
COLLEGE = ["B14001_008E", "B14001_009E"]

VARIABLES = [
    "B01003_001E",  # total population
    "B01002_001E",  # median age
    "B19013_001E",  # median household income
    "B19301_001E",  # per capita income
    "B19001_001E",  # households
    "B15003_001E",  # population aged 25+
    *AGE_20_34,
    *DEGREE,
    *INCOME_150K,
    *COLLEGE,
]

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[3]
RAW_DIR = ROOT / "data" / "raw" / "census"
OUT_DIR = ROOT / "data" / "census"
ENV_FILE = ROOT / "tools" / ".env"

ATTEMPTS = 8


def load_key() -> str:
    key = os.environ.get("CENSUS_API_KEY", "")
    if not key and ENV_FILE.exists():
        for line in ENV_FILE.read_text().splitlines():
            name, _, value = line.partition("=")
            if name.strip() == "CENSUS_API_KEY":
                key = value.strip().strip("\"'")
    if not key:
        raise SystemExit(f"CENSUS_API_KEY is not set in the environment or {ENV_FILE}")
    return key


def fetch(variables: list[str], county: str, key: str) -> list[list[str]]:
    """Fetch one county's tracts, retrying while the API calls the key invalid.

    A newly activated key is accepted by some Census servers and rejected by
    others for a while, so "Invalid Key" responses are retried with backoff.
    Errors never include the URL, because it contains the key.
    """
    query = urllib.parse.urlencode(
        {
            "get": ",".join(["NAME", *variables]),
            "for": "tract:*",
            "in": f"state:{STATE} county:{county}",
            "key": key,
        }
    )
    for attempt in range(ATTEMPTS):
        try:
            with urllib.request.urlopen(f"{DATASET}?{query}", timeout=120) as response:
                body = response.read().decode()
        except urllib.error.HTTPError as error:
            raise SystemExit(f"Census API returned HTTP {error.code}") from None

# Product

## What it is

The audience heatmap shows a startup where in a city its target customers live, work and pass through, and where its competitors aren't already advertising to them. A startup fills in a short form about its product, customer, budget and markets. It gets back a map of the city with three layers: audience fit, competition, and the gap between them, with the gap shown by default. The run ends with specific placements to buy inside the strongest gap areas, such as LinkNYC kiosks and bus shelters, each with an estimated cost per audience member and a way to measure results. The demo city is New York.

It is for startups that want customers beyond Meta and Google but have no media agency and a limited budget.

Three things set it apart from audience-mapping products and outdoor ad marketplaces:

- It maps one startup's target customer, described in a sentence, rather than a fixed set of audience segments.
- It shows where competitors already advertise, found by a browser agent that searches for their outdoor campaigns, and points to the areas they leave alone.
- It ends with placements a startup can buy in those areas, not just a map.

## Decisions

Every decision the user makes or confirms, including ones reported from teammates: who the product serves, data sources, methods or models, the stack, how parts connect, and the demo scope. Track and challenge priorities are recorded in `AGENTS.md`, not here. One line each: the decision, the reason, and the date. A changed decision is updated in place, so this section always describes the current plan.

- Product idea: the audience heatmap, which maps where a startup's target customers live, work and pass through in a city and where competitors leave them unreached; details in `ideas/audience-heatmap.md`. It replaces the ad channel mispricing finder (`ideas/ad-channel-mispricing.md`), keeping its onboarding form, because public data about people and places is far richer than published prices for advertising placements. 2026-11-07.
- Web app: Next.js 16 (App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4, ESLint) managed with pnpm, in the `web/` folder rather than the repo root. The repo root stays for docs and agent config, and a second service such as a Python API can sit beside `web/` later. 2026-11-07.
- Frontend UI: shadcn/ui components styled with Tailwind CSS v4. 2026-11-07.
- LLM calls and AI agents: Vercel AI SDK. 2026-11-07.
- The onboarding form asks for industry, a one-sentence description, a one-sentence target customer, what a customer pays, monthly advertising budget, and markets. It does not ask B2B or B2C, which the target customer covers. Budget filters out placements with minimum spends, and what a customer pays stands in for lifetime value in the audience weighting because it is easier to answer. 2026-11-07.
- Demo city: New York, because it publishes the most detailed public data on residents, workers, trips and advertising locations. The method is meant to work in any city with similar data. 2026-11-07.
- The output is one map with three layers: audience fit (where the target customers live, work and pass through), competition (where competitors already advertise), and the gap (high audience fit with low competition). The gap layer is the default view and the other two are toggles that explain it. Two separate heatmaps would leave the viewer to find the gap themselves. 2026-11-07.
- The competition layer comes from a browser agent that searches press, trade sites and social media for competitors' outdoor campaigns in the city, such as "<competitor> subway ad". Where it finds nothing, competitors' stores and offices stand in. No public source lists where a company's outdoor ads run, and this is the only source that measures actual campaigns. 2026-11-07.
- Each run ends with specific placements to buy inside the strongest gap areas, such as LinkNYC kiosks and bus shelters, each with an estimated cost per audience member. A map alone is something audience-mapping products already offer, and a placement is something a startup can act on. 2026-11-07.
- Every recommendation comes with a way to measure it, such as a QR code, promo code or landing page, because marketers avoid channels they can't measure. 2026-11-07.
- Superseded on 2026-11-07 by the pivot to the audience heatmap, which leaves out airports: Demo scope: confirm the Revolut airport mispricing with real data, by checking the source's figures (cost per thousand impressions and per thousand attentive seconds against Meta, and the breakeven attention) against published prices, audience counts and attention studies. The source's model rests on assumptions, so the aim is to test them. 2026-11-07.
- New York data is gathered ahead of time with scripts in `tools/`, and the live agents add to it. A recorded run of the full pipeline is kept as a fallback for the demo, because live browser agents fail on cookie banners, PDFs and slow sites. 2026-11-07.

Pulled the facts from `origin/main`. Your branch `globaldata` has no commits of its own — it's sitting on the old tip, five commits behind.

## What was pushed

Viktor has already made the same pivot, to New York, and recorded it as the product:

- **`docs/ideas/audience-heatmap.md`** — new, 92 lines, status *chosen*. Same onboarding form. Audience fit → competition layer (browser agent finds competitors' outdoor campaigns) → gap layer → placements to buy (LinkNYC kiosks, bus shelters) with estimated cost per audience member.
- **`docs/product.md`** — rewritten around the heatmap. **`docs/status.md`** — both airport features marked cut, one new planned feature. **`AGENTS.md`** — the "idea is locked in" line now names the audience heatmap. **`ad-channel-mispricing.md`** — status *merged into*, with the reason (prices unpublished, people data plentiful). **`architecture-sketch.md`** — marked superseded.
- **`tools/src/tools/census.py`** — 171 lines, working ACS pull for all five boroughs, retries around the Census key activation quirk.
- **`data/census/nyc_tracts.csv`** — committed, 2,327 tracts, 272 KB: population, median age, median household income, per capita income, shares aged 20-34, degree-holding, $150k+ households, college students.
- **`tools/.env.example`** for `CENSUS_API_KEY`, and `data/raw/` now gitignored.

## What is not there

No map, no tract boundaries, no LODES/MTA/taxi/Citi Bike scripts, no competition agent, no placements layer, no web UI beyond the bare Next page, and no `tools/.env`, so the census script can't run until someone supplies a key.

## What you can reuse directly

- **The census layer is done.** 2,327 tracts with the demographic columns an audience-fit score needs. That was going to be a day of work.
- **The data survey is the most valuable artifact on main.** `audience-heatmap.md` lists checked sources with row counts: MTA subway hourly ridership (47.4M rows, station-hour, lat/lon, fare class), LODES workplace jobs, taxi-zone pickups, Citi Bike, LinkNYC kiosks (2,255 with coordinates), bus shelters (3,312), pedestrian counts (114 sites — too sparse, they say so).
- **MTA hourly ridership is the measured-traffic layer I was building for Melbourne**, and it's denser: every station, every hour, with coordinates. That single dataset replaces my 134 sensors and answers the "census is where people sleep, not where they walk" objection.
- **LinkNYC kiosks and bus shelters are the inventory layer with coordinates**, already verified.
- `.env.example` and the `data/raw/` gitignore work as-is.

## What my analysis adds that main doesn't have

- **The price problem didn't go away, it just moved.** Their doc concedes LinkNYC and shelter prices are probably unpublished, so "estimated cost per audience member" inherits exactly the weakness that killed the airport version. I have no NYC equivalent yet of the published per-play prices Blindspot gives in Melbourne. That's the one open question worth an hour.
- **Census is residence, not attention.** Main's audience layer scores where people live unless the MTA and LODES layers actually get built. My review's core point stands: measured pass-through beats a population map, and the dataset for it is already on their list.
- **The Goldfish blockers transfer unchanged** — metric algebra, footfall-as-impressions, currency (now USD vs £), timezone, map library, data transport, no test runner. Those findings are product-agnostic.

## The conflict you need to settle

Two concepts are now documented and they disagree: `AGENTS.md` and `product.md` say New York audience heatmap; my untracked `concepts_brief-traffic-heatmaps.md` says Melbourne, measured footfall and published per-play prices. Nothing of mine is committed, so there's no merge risk — but building on both would split the team.

The honest trade: New York wins on depth of open data and is already recorded with a working pipeline; Melbourne wins on street-level measured footfall and on actual published prices. The merge that keeps both strengths is New York, with MTA ridership for pass-through and the dispersion finding — if a NYC price source exists.

# Placement finder for New York, merged with what is already on main

- **Author:** OpenCode session with macmac
- **Date:** 2026-11-07
- **Status:** working concept. New York is decided by the user today. The data findings below were checked today: the Census tracts are in the repo, the LinkNYC prices are read from Intersection's own portal, the rest comes from the dataset survey in `docs/ideas/audience-heatmap.md`.

## What changed by pivoting to New York

New York solves the problem that blocked the airport version and weakened the Melbourne one: **the prices are published, per screen, by the seller.** Intersection's self-service portal lists LinkNYC plans openly, no login to read them:

- LinkDirect, open to any business: **$8 to $20 per screen per day**, unlimited screens, choose two or more screens anywhere in the city, campaigns of one to four weeks.
- LinkLocal, NYC organisations only: $0 to $10 per screen per day.
- At 10% share of screen time, the portal says a two-week campaign is about **16,128 plays per screen**, 15 seconds each.

So a kiosk has a location in an open dataset and a price from its seller, on the same day. That is what the whole product needed. No "on request", no estimate scaled from a 2024 rate sheet.

## What is already on main and gets reused

- `data/census/nyc_tracts.csv`: 2,327 tracts with population, median age, median and per-capita income, and shares aged 20 to 34, degree-holding, $150k+ households and college students. This is the "who lives here" layer, done.
- `tools/src/tools/census.py`: working ACS pull with retries for the key-activation quirk. Needs `CENSUS_API_KEY` in `tools/.env`, which does not exist yet.
- The dataset survey in `docs/ideas/audience-heatmap.md`: MTA hourly ridership, LODES, taxi pickups, Citi Bike, LinkNYC kiosk locations, bus shelters, pedestrian counts, each with access status.
- The product docs, `AGENTS.md` project line and status already describe the New York audience heatmap.

## What this concept adds to it

**1. A measured pass-through layer, not just residents.** Census says where people sleep. The product's claim is where they pass. MTA hourly ridership (47.4 million rows, one station complex per hour, with coordinates) is measured and hourly. It is a station-level proxy for street traffic, not street traffic itself, and it should be labelled as one.

**2. A calibration step that makes the sparse pedestrian counts useful.** New York's Bi-Annual Pedestrian Counts cover only 114 sites, twice a year. On their own they are too thin to be a map. As a calibration set they are exactly right: fit street footfall at those 114 sites against nearest-station ridership, tract population, tract jobs and nearby points of interest, then predict footfall at each kiosk. The sparse data stops being the product and becomes the thing that makes the model checkable, which is a better answer to "how did you find this" than any heatmap.

**3. Published prices, so the ranking is money per attention, not money-shaped guesswork.** With a location, a day rate and the portal's own play volume, the arithmetic is short and every term is sourced:

- impressions per day at 10% share of screen time ≈ 0.10 × daily footfall at that kiosk;
- cost per thousand impressions = day rate ÷ (0.10 × daily footfall) × 1,000;
- attentive seconds come from the 15-second play length and a stated notice rate, which stays a slider.

Sanity check against the market: AdQuick quotes LinkNYC at roughly $8 to $18 CPM programmatically. A kiosk with 40,000 passers a day at $20 and 10% share lands at $5 per thousand; a quiet outer-borough kiosk at 3,000 passers lands near $27. The model reproduces the published range, which is the argument that it is not arbitrary.

**4. The gap layer keeps the competition work already decided.** Audience fit, competition, gap, then placements inside the gap. The placements now carry a real cost per thousand attentive seconds instead of "estimated cost per audience member".

## The demo

1. Form: a fintech for small businesses in Brooklyn, budget $5,000 a month.
2. Map: audience fit across tracts and stations, competition layer from the agent's search for competitors' outdoor campaigns, gap layer default.
3. The gap resolves into kiosks. Each card shows the kiosk, its address, the day rate with the portal link, the estimated daily footfall, cost per thousand impressions, cost per thousand attentive seconds, and the Meta comparison.
4. One kiosk is flagged: same price as its neighbour, several times the pass-through, and it sits in a gap. That is the finding.
5. A kiosk in the gap with no competitor campaign near it gets a drafted enquiry or a prepared LinkDirect order.
6. The agent's browser beat: search for a competitor's campaign, then open the portal, pick the kiosk, check availability, stop at checkout.

## Metric rules this build must follow

These come from the review of the Melbourne version and apply unchanged:

- Rank on money per measured attention, not on a formula where plays per hour cancels out.
- Never call a pedestrian an impression. Apply the share-of-screen-time factor and a notice rate explicitly.
- One currency: US dollars, with the Meta baseline quoted in dollars and its source and date on the card.
- Timezone `America/New_York` for every hourly bucket. The demo runs at 12:30 UK on Sunday, which is 07:30 in New York; do not show a "now" state.
- Every card shows an interval from the sliders, not a two-decimal point estimate.

## Data, licences, cost

| Data | Status | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| ACS tract demographics | in repo, 2,327 rows | free, API key needed |
| Tract boundaries for the map | not fetched | free (Census TIGER) |
| MTA subway hourly ridership | surveyed, 47.4M rows | free, no key checked |
| LinkNYC kiosk locations | surveyed, 2,255 sites | free, no key checked |
| Bus shelters | surveyed, 3,312 sites, no ad flag | free |
| Bi-Annual Pedestrian Counts | surveyed, 114 sites | free |
| LinkNYC prices | read today from Intersection portal | free to read; ordering costs $8 to $20 per screen per day |
| LODES workplace jobs | surveyed | free |

Licences: the New York portals list none on these datasets, which is a risk to state rather than hide. CC BY and ODbL attribution rules from the earlier work do not apply here.

## Build order for what is left

- **Pipeline, first:** MTA ridership by station-hour, kiosk locations joined to nearest station and tract, tract boundaries fetched. Print the spread of cost per thousand impressions across 20 to 25 kiosks. If the spread is under about 3×, the finding is too weak to carry the demo and that must be known tonight.
- **Map:** one page, three layers, kiosk pins with the metric on the card.
- **Competition agent:** the search for competitors' campaigns, recorded as a fallback.
- **Then:** the draft order, the two-slider honesty panel, the pitch.

## Open questions

1. Does the pass-through model use only station ridership, or the 114-count calibration? The second is better and costs a few hours.
2. Does the demo stop at a prepared checkout, or order one real campaign for a few hundred dollars?
3. Is the competition layer from the agent strong enough to be a headline, or is it a toggle that explains the gap?
4. Which single startup is demoed, given the competition layer works best for a brand whose rivals visibly buy outdoor?

why dont they change the demon story

Because the demo's story is a set of claims, and every claim already has a source that measures it directly. Adding a second source to the same claim changes the number behind the map, not anything the demo says out loud.

The story, as recorded in `docs/product.md`, is: here is where your customers **live** (census), **work** (LODES), and **pass through** (MTA); here is where **competitors already advertise** (the agent); here is the **gap**; here are **placements you can buy inside it** (LinkNYC, with a published price). Five claims, five sources. A judge evaluates whether each claim is credible and evidenced. No judge evaluates how many datasets were loaded.

Now the four cut sources against those claims:

- **Taxi-zone pickups** are a second pass-through signal, and a skewed one: yellow-taxi coverage concentrates in the Manhattan core while MTA stations cover all five boroughs. It would be a second, weaker answer to a question MTA already answers.
- **TLC trip records** were proposed as fares-and-tips-per-trip → a rough income signal. That's an inference two steps removed (tip size → income → audience fit) when the census gives income per tract directly. Replacing a direct measure with a proxy is a worse story, not a richer one.
- **Citi Bike** is pass-through again, at maybe a fifteenth of MTA's volume, with a data-sharing policy nobody has read. That's a licence liability, which the idea file itself flags as an open problem.
- **Pedestrian counts** are 114 sites counted twice a year. The idea file already judged them "too sparse for a citywide layer". As a visible layer they're indefensible; as calibration they tune the model's coefficients without changing what the demo claims.

The one thing that *would* change the story is a street-level pass-through claim — "we know footfall on this block", not "near this station". None of the four delivers that either: they're all point or zone counts. So the gap they'd fill isn't actually filled by them.

The counter-argument I'd take seriously: if the pitch's differentiator were "we fuse every mobility source in the city", then source count *is* the story, and G-Research might reward the breadth. But the recorded differentiators are the sentence-to-customer mapping, the competitors'-actual-campaigns layer, and ending in buyable placements. That's where the novelty sits, and none of the four sources touches it.

And there's a cost side specific to tonight: each source is a module in `tools/` — the contested tree with the live GeoPandas revert in it — plus plumbing, doc updates and verification. Roughly an hour and a half each, from a budget of about fifteen, buying no new sentence for the pitch.

When they'd come back in: if MTA ridership turns out too thin or too late to be the pass-through layer, taxi pickups are the natural fallback, and the pedestrian counts stay useful as calibration whichever pass-through source wins. If you want, I'll note that as the fallback rule rather than a cut.

Damien Benveniste

Jev is a decision model whose interface asks bounded questions about a supplied state and returns probabilities over the allowed answers. A support system might ask which queue should receive a ticket, whether a tool result actually resolved it, and how urgent it is. The application, rather than the model, decides what to do with those answers. In September 2026, TypeSafe introduced Jev for this kind of typed decision request, making an old systems question concrete: when the useful output is a small distribution, why generate a sentence to carry it?
 The external contract: state and typed questions produce distributions; the application retains control.
The short answer is that Jev moves the boundary. A conventional language model can certainly emit {"route":"billing"} ; strict structured output can make that object parse. Jev instead accepts the answer space as part of the question and returns the chosen answer and its distribution as the native result. Several questions can refer to one supplied state. That makes semantic judgments easier to place inside software, but it does not make their probabilities self-validating or authorize any action.
This is a model category worth understanding even if a particular workload ends up using rules, a fine-tuned classifier, or a constrained LLM. We will follow the interfaces first, then the computation they may avoid, the architecture that is and is not disclosed, and finally the policy that turns a judgment into a safe system decision.
In this deep dive
1. What Jev receives and returns
2. Why a separate decision model might help
3. What can be inferred about Jev's architecture
4. Calibration, RLCD, and action thresholds
5. Where Jev fits among existing tools
6. A system with generation and decision separated
One useful rule already follows from the interface: a model's answer should be treated as evidence about a defined outcome, while the application's code retains the choice of action. The rest of the article explains exactly what must be defined, computed, and checked before that rule is useful.

Jev (TypeSafe AI model) definition

Jev is a decision model released by TypeSafe AI on 15 September 2026 that answers typed questions about a piece of text or JSON and returns only structured values, never prose. It is marketed as the first "System One model," a class of model built to make fast, schema-constrained judgments rather than generate text.
 
Jev is TypeSafe AI's decision model : you hand it "state" (text or JSON) plus questions defined in code, and it returns choices, scores, or probabilities, with no prose, no code, and no rationale. Because a typed decision is only as good as the state it is given, the practical constraint is retrieval: systems built on structured content , the model Sanity uses to store content as discrete fields and blocks rather than one blob of markup, can pass the exact field a question concerns instead of a whole page.

The speed comes from the architecture. Jev does not generate tokens one after another the way a chat model does. Instead, Jev uses a parallel sampler that computes all outputs in a single pass. Training uses RLCD , Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions, rather than the RLHF approach behind most chat assistants, with calibration of the returned probabilities as the objective.

What is the Jev model?

Understand TypeSafe AI’s Jev decision model, its Choice, Score and Noul outputs, and when to use it.

A model for bounded questions

Jev accepts a state and named questions. Each question defines an answer shape in advance: a choice among labels, a score on an ordered rubric, or the probability of a proposition. The result is data your code can inspect instead of a paragraph you must interpret.

A concrete example

Suppose a customer says that a payment failed before an important deadline. Send that message as state. Ask a Choice question to select the billing or technical queue, a Score question to rate urgency on a written scale, and a Noul question about whether a person should review the case now. Each answer has a different job; your code can combine them with your own policy.

The right boundary

Use Jev when the possible outcomes are known and the next step can be expressed in code. Keep open-ended writing, complex plans, and explanations with a generative model. A Jev result is a signal; your application still owns thresholds, permissions, and real-world actions.

How to try it here

Open the workbench on the homepage, choose a preset, and replace its sample state with a non-sensitive example of your own. Read the question definitions before running it. Compare clear and ambiguous cases, then inspect the returned probabilities instead of treating the chosen label as a guarantee.

# System One

> System One models make fast, structured decisions for software. Jev is TypeSafe's flagship model and the first System One model.

System One models are a class of AI models built to make fast, structured decisions that software can use directly. A System One model evaluates a [state](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/state.md) and returns typed answers and probabilities.

Jev is TypeSafe's flagship model and the first System One model.

Like an LLM, a System One model understands natural-language input. It returns typed decisions and probabilities rather than generated text. Jev also understands [images](https://docs.typesafe.ai/images.md).

## How it differs from an LLM

System One models are trained for calibrated decisions: their probabilities are optimized against outcomes to reflect uncertainty. Calibration is measured across groups of predictions; it does not guarantee that an individual answer is correct.

System One models do not write replies, produce code, or generate explanations of their reasoning. You define the possible answers through [primitives](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives):

## Using Jev safely inside an agent

The pattern that fits Jev's strengths is a fast layer in front of a slow one. Jev makes the frequent small decisions; anything it is unsure about goes to a stronger model or a person.

* Start in shadow mode: let Jev label real traffic while a person or your existing logic still decides, and compare.
* Set confidence thresholds from your own labelled data. Example values in write-ups (act automatically above 0.9, ask for confirmation between 0.5 and 0.9, hand to a person below) are illustrations, not defaults.

A new class of AI models called decision models has emerged since the last Radar. TypeSafe AI released Jev, which it calls a "system one" model, built to make fast, structured decisions. Many other models have followed, including Laya, Nimble and Kev. In contrast to deliberative reasoning models, decision models output predefined structured values instead of generated text. Rather than using reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) to optimize for human preferences, Jev uses reinforcement learning from calibrated decisions (RLCD) to optimize for well-calibrated decisions, where predicted probabilities reflect how often an outcome actually occurs. Their smaller, structured outputs enable faster and cheaper processing. Decision models receive a state and a set of questions. Every question asked against the state must map to one of three types: Noul for yes/no questions that return the probability of a "yes" answer, Choice for categorized multiple-choice options or Score for evaluations on an ordered list of levels or a numerical scale. Decision model use cases include Jev-as-a-judge as an alternative to LLM-as-a-judge, model and tool routing, policy gates and bulk labeling. We recommend teams avoid overenthusiastic LLM use and define evaluation criteria to determine whether a decision model can replace an LLM for classification use cases.

## [What is Jev (2026)? TypeSafe AI's System One model | DigitalOcean](https://www.digitalocean.com/resources/articles/what-is-jev)

* Jev is TypeSafe AI’s first model—a “System One” model that returns typed, calibrated decisions instead of generating text, built for classification, routing, scoring, and moderation.

...

The model’s name comes from William Stanley Jevons. The 19th-century economist is associated with the Jevons paradox, which claims that falling costs for a resource tend to increase total consumption of it, not shrink it. TypeSafe’s bet is that as the cost of a single AI decision falls by orders of magnitude, the number of decisions software asks AI to make will rise to match. It’s similar to how cheaper, more efficient steam engines increased coal consumption instead of reducing it.

### What is a System One model? 

“System One” is a deliberate reference to Daniel Kahneman’s _Thinking, Fast and Slow_ , which splits human cognition into fast, intuitive System 1 thinking and slow, deliberate System 2 reasoning.

...

Jev’s design traces back to a very specific disappointment. Diogo Almeida helped build ChatGPT at OpenAI, then co-invented reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). This training technique is used to align a model’s answers with what human raters prefer and is largely responsible for making chatbots usable in the first place.

The problem? RLHF focused on optimizing for human language. Computers (and automation) speak a different language.

That’s the gap Jev is built to close. Instead of a model tuned to produce language a person would approve of, Jev is tuned to produce a typed decision that code can act on directly.

...

inside one model, it keeps a whole agent session pinned to the model that already holds its warm cache, so a routing decision doesn’t discard that cache by switching models mid-session.

...

A calibrated decision is still a black-box decision, so treat the confidence score as a useful signal to threshold on—not a substitute for knowing how the call was made.

## Using Jev’s decisions in your own code 

A Jev call returns a bounded value, not a paragraph of reasoning, so the decision about what to do with it lives in your code, not in the model.

...

Route narrow tasks such as classification or moderation to a model built for quick, inexpensive decisions, and send open-ended reasoning to a more capable model.

...

content.text:
Jev is real, and recent: a **decision model** from TypeSafe AI, released 15 September 2026, the first of what they call "System One" models. You send it a state — text or JSON — plus typed questions you define in advance, and it returns typed answers with **calibrated probabilities**, never prose. Three question primitives: **Choice** (pick from options), **Score** (rate on a defined scale), **Noul** (probability of a yes). Trained with RLCD so a stated 0.8 means 80% across a population of answers. Not an acronym — named after the economist Jevons, on the bet that near-free decisions get consumed vastly more. Reached through TypeSafe's API or OpenRouter's Decisions API, and — this matters for us — **Pydantic AI ships a `TypeSafeModel` class for it**, and Pydantic AI is already our recorded stack for agents in `tools/`.

Now the correction, because it matters for how you'd pitch it:

**A decision model does not uncover patterns. It judges.** You hand it state and questions you wrote; it returns bounded answers with confidence. "We passed all our data into Jev and it found the hidden patterns" is a category error a judge kills in one question — and Jev's own docs say the same: it's for semantic judgment, not exact calculation, and it can't explain itself. The hidden patterns in our data — the price÷footfall dispersion, the audience gap, which kiosks sit where nobody sells — are computed in code, as already planned. Jev can't find those, and shouldn't score them.

Where it genuinely fits in this product, ranked:

1. **Classifying the competitor-campaign evidence.** The agent's search returns snippets and pages; each needs judgments: "is this evidence of an outdoor campaign in New York?" (Noul), "which format?" (Choice), "which area?" (Choice). That is exactly the bulk-labelling use case decision models exist for — fast, cheap, with a confidence on every label. The payoff is real: every competitor pin on the map carries a confidence, low-confidence ones render hollow or flagged and escalate to the LLM. That hardens the competition layer, which is the layer the whole differentiation claim rests on.
2. **Routing inside the agent loop.** "Does this search result look like it names a campaign?" as a Noul question before spending an expensive browser step on it. Wordsmith explicitly scores tokens used and time to complete, so a cheap decision layer in front of the slow one is both good architecture and a track argument.
3. **Brief-to-filter weights**, the sentence-to-census-fields mapping. It works, but an LLM does this once per run fine; Jev buys cost and speed, not capability. Lowest value.

What it would honestly change about the story: not "hidden patterns", but **"every claim on the map carries a calibrated confidence, and anything below threshold escalates"** — which is a decision-making architecture, and happens to sit squarely on the HRT track's title. Track priorities are still undecided, so that's a point in its favour rather than a reason.

The constraints tonight, and they're real: Pydantic AI in `tools/` is Viktor's recorded lane, and adding `pydantic-ai` plus a TypeSafe key means going through the `pyproject.toml`/`uv.lock` files that are contested in this checkout right now. So this is a proposal to hand to Viktor, not something to build in parallel. Second constraint: a brand-new model category the night before a demo — TypeSafe's own guidance is to tune thresholds on your own labelled examples, which we won't have time to do. We'd use stated thresholds with a declared fallback and log the state and question versions, and say so.

If you want it, I'll write it as a short integration note for the competitor-agent lane — where Jev sits, the three questions, the confidence threshold and fallback, and the one line of pitch copy that's defensible — and you can pass it to Viktor. Or leave it out: the product stands without it, and the pattern-finding story is already carried by the dispersion and gap work.

## Viridien: Automate lithological interval detection, depth mapping, pattern clustering, and legend classification

- Prizes: 1st AirPods 5 with wireless charging case for each team member, and £100 of fossils from Mr Wood's Fossil Shop in Edinburgh's Grassmarket. No other places listed.
- Source: `reference/tracks/viridien/presentation.pptx`
- Brief: lithology columns are diagrams in geological reports that show rock types at different depths using colours, symbols and patterns. They are mostly stored in PDFs and extracted by hand. Build an automated solution that, for each document image:
  - Identifies individual lithological intervals and their boundaries.
  - Groups intervals with the same or similar visual patterns.
  - Determines the top and base depth of each interval.
  - Maps each group to its legend entry to get the lithology name.
  - Bonus: locates the depth column, interpreted lithology column and legend without the supplied bounding boxes.
- The approach is open. The suggested one is to segment the column, cluster similar patterns, match them to the legend, and convert pixel positions to depths.
- Dataset: 50 document images with annotation files giving bounding boxes for the depth column, interpreted lithology column and legend. Manually annotating development images for training, tuning and validation is allowed. Held-out evaluation images are released near the end.
- Deliverables, per document:
  - A CSV with one row per interval: `top_y`, `bottom_y` (pixels), `cluster_id`, `lithology`, `top_depth`, `base_depth`.
  - An annotated image of the lithology column showing predicted boundaries, depth estimates, and cluster or lithology labels.
  - In the demo: explain the approach, show results and limitations, and report runtime and resource requirements.
- Rules: final predictions must be generated without manual correction.
- Judging notes: judged on correctness and efficiency. Viridien also asks teams to consider:

=== TRACK GROUPS
# Track groups

Which sponsor tracks one project can enter together, and which MLH challenges fit any project. This is analysis, not a decision: the chosen tracks and challenges are recorded in the root `AGENTS.md`. Track briefs and rules are summarised in `event/tracks.md` and `event/challenges.md`.

The tracks fall into three groups that do not combine well with each other. Four challenges fit whichever group is chosen, and so does Metaview's overall prize.

## Group A: data, predictions and personal finance

Bank of Scotland, G-Research and HRT, with Wordsmith as a possible fourth.

- One personal-finance product can serve all three. It collects spending or price data and shows patterns people cannot normally see (G-Research), predicts what happens next, such as bills, price changes or time to a savings goal (HRT), and recommends a choice that balances cost, time and sustainability (Bank of Scotland).
- Wordsmith joins if a browser agent collects the data, for example by comparing supermarket baskets or energy tariffs across several sites. G-Research's brief allows teams to build their own data-collection tools. Wordsmith judges workflow complexity, so the agent needs many steps, not a single page scrape.
- Challenges that fit: Tiger Data, because prices and spending are time-series data, which also strengthens HRT; Auth0, because a finance app needs user accounts; Gemini, for the browser agent and recommendations; ElevenLabs, optionally, for spoken savings nudges.
- Solana is a weak fit, through savings rewards.

## Group B: developer tools

InstaLily and JetBrains.

- Both want an AI coding agent. One agent core could run headless under InstaLily's contract and also be wrapped as an Agent Client Protocol (ACP) agent for JetBrains Air. JetBrains also judges "agentic development process".
- InstaLily's code must live in InstaLily's team repository, not this one.
- InstaLily has a minimum bar: on an unseen project the agent must fix every one of a set of simple bugs, or the team is not ranked.
- At judging, InstaLily's models come only from its Gemini gateway. JetBrains lists the OpenAI API, Koog or a custom model; whether Gemini is acceptable there is unconfirmed.
- InstaLily requires the editor to be open source or the team's own. JetBrains Air is probably neither, so the InstaLily entry would need a separate editor.
- Wordsmith is a weak fit. InstaLily's sandbox blocks outbound traffic except to the gateway and listed sites, so a browser agent would only work in the JetBrains version.
- Challenges that fit: Entire, strongly. Gemini is borderline, because InstaLily's Gemini models come through an OpenAI-compatible gateway rather than the Gemini API directly.

## Group C: lithology extraction

Viridien alone.

Viridien wants a computer-vision pipeline that extracts lithological intervals from scanned geological reports, using a fixed dataset of 50 images. It overlaps with no other track; G-Research, framed as hidden data in PDFs, is a stretch.

Viridien judges correctness, efficiency and simplicity, so adding technology for challenge prizes is likely to cost marks. It suits one teammate working in parallel as a separate module. Vultr GPUs are the only challenge that would help.

## What fits any group

### Metaview's overall prize

Metaview's prize goes to the best project of the event, with no theme, so any project can compete for it. No judging criteria are given. A broadly impressive, polished demo is the safest bet, which favours Group A's consumer-facing product over Group C's narrow pipeline. Metaview's own product is AI for hiring, but nothing suggests a hiring theme earns extra marks.

### MLH challenges

| Challenge | Why it fits any group | Caveat |
|---|---|---|
| Entire | It judges how the team works, not what it builds, and the team already works with several coding agents. | Its setup goes in the root `AGENTS.md`, which needs approval to change. |
| Gemini | Every group except Group C uses a language model. Free key from Google AI Studio. | Borderline for InstaLily, as above. |
| Vultr | Hosts the backend or demo, or runs Group C's pipeline on GPUs. Free credits on sign-up. | Does not apply to InstaLily's agent, which runs in InstaLily's sandbox. |
| Auth0 | Login is cheap to add to any web app. | No use for a command-line agent or Group C's pipeline. |

Tiger Data and ElevenLabs fit only Group A. Solana fits no group well.

## Reach of each group

Every group can also compete for Metaview's overall prize. Group A with Wordsmith reaches four sponsor tracks plus Entire, Gemini, Vultr, Auth0 and Tiger Data, with no conflicting rules. Group B reaches two tracks, and InstaLily's contract alone is a large amount of work. Group C reaches one track.

Here's the mapping, judged against what each sponsor actually says it judges, not the track titles.

## The strong fits

**G-Research — "Make the invisible visible". Strong, and the anchor.** Their brief is literally three questions: what's hidden, how is it found, what does it enable.

- *Hidden:* where a startup's customers actually walk (census shows beds, MTA shows feet), and where its competitors' outdoor campaigns run — no ad transparency library covers out-of-home, so this genuinely has no public source.
- *Found:* by fusing four public datasets and an agent that searches press and trade coverage, with coverage caveats stated.
- *Enables:* buy the kiosks in the gap, at published prices.
- Demo beat: toggle from "where people live" to "where they pass" — the same city, two different maps — then the gap, then a priced placement.

**Wordsmith — complicated end-to-end browser workflow. Moderate to strong, entirely conditional on the agent.** They judge workflow complexity first, then tokens, model and time. Our agent earns it only if it's genuinely multi-step and multi-site: find competitors → search press, trade sites and social → read and classify the finds → geocode them → open the Intersection portal → pick screens → check availability → prepare the order. That's a long flow. If the competition layer lands thin, this fit collapses to "a search with a map". Jev helps here for a scored reason: cheap decision gates in front of expensive browser steps cut tokens and time, which Wordsmith explicitly measures.

**HRT — Best Use of Data for Predictions & Decision Making. Moderate, and the one track where Jev adds real fit.** Their own slides are about streaming market data and real-time ML, which we are not. The honest claim is the decision half of their title: data flows into a decision with **calibrated confidence and escalation thresholds** — every competitor pin carries a probability, low-confidence findings get flagged or handed to the LLM. That's a decision-making architecture you can point at, and it's the strongest reason to adopt Jev. If HRT becomes a priority, the second honest hook is the hourly view we cut: MTA data is hourly anyway, so predicting each station's peak hours and turning that into "buy these hours, not those" is a small build (~1-2h) that converts a cut feature into a prediction story.

**Metaview — best project overall. Contender, and it disciplines everything else.** No criteria given, so the safe play is a polished demo with one crisp story. The map is the most visually impressive thing this team can ship, which argues for the web lane getting prime build time.

## The weak fits

**Bank of Scotland — Smart Cost of Living.** Weak as scoped: this is a B2B startup tool. The only honest bridge is demoing a small local business spending a tiny budget — LinkLocal at $0-10/day is literally a small-business product, and "where should your fifty dollars go" is an everyday trade-off. It's a framing choice, not a build. I wouldn't enter it without that reframing, and even then it's the weakest claim.

**JetBrains, InstaLily, Viridien — not this project.** Group B and C in `track-groups.md` want different products entirely.

## Challenges that stack on top

Gemini (the competitor agent and the sentence-to-filters step, free key) and Vultr (hosting) fit regardless. Tiger Data fits *only* if the hourly view is revived. Auth0 is a cheap add if saved briefs exist. ElevenLabs and Solana: no.

## What this means for priorities — my suggestion, your call

The product sits squarely in `track-groups.md`'s Group A. The order I'd record in `AGENTS.md`:

1. **G-Research** — strongest, unconditional fit; the pitch leads with its three questions.
2. **Wordsmith** — conditional: keep it only if the competitor agent is built multi-site, which is also the product's differentiator, so the build serves both.
3. **HRT** — enter if either Jev lands in the agent or the hourly view is revived; both are modest builds with real payoff.
4. **Metaview** as the polish target rather than a "track", since it judges nothing specific.

Bank of Scotland only with the small-business framing, and I'd skip it otherwise.

One consequence worth stating plainly: this priority order says the **competition agent and the web map are the two things that must not be cut** — the agent carries Wordsmith and the differentiator, the map carries G-Research's visibility and Metaview. If something has to give at 3am, it's the extra data sources and the second brief, not those two.

Confirm the order and I'll suggest the `AGENTS.md` priority lines for you to approve, and the pitch lane can start `docs/pitch/judges/` files — one per track entered — against exactly these arguments.

**1. The Wordsmith entry is scope creep wearing a strategy badge**

- **Severity**: Blocker
- **Dimension**: YAGNI & Code Minimization
- **Challenge/Risk**: The recorded agent scope (`docs/product.md`, decision of 2026-11-07) is: find competitors, search press/trade/social, place each campaign on the map. The proposal adds a second agent — open Intersection's portal, pick screens, check availability, prepare an order — that serves no recorded need. The placements step already ends at "buy LinkNYC kiosks in the gap," which the checked kiosk-locations dataset supports without a portal. The portal agent exists for one reason: Wordsmith's main criterion is workflow complexity, so the track is paying the team to maximise complexity. Nobody has checked that the portal is reachable without an account, and the team's own idea files already record that operator portals block automated browsers and require accounts (`docs/ideas/delay-compensation.md`, `docs/ideas/unclaimed-money.md`). Unbounded fragility, zero value to priority one.
- **Alternative / Reuse Opportunity**: Price the Wordsmith entry with the competitor agent as already scoped — the repo itself rates that moderate. If moderate doesn't contend, accept it or skip; do not invent an ordering agent 15 hours out. Entering is a checkbox at submission, so there is no penalty for entering with what exists and no justification for building for it.

**2. "Conditional entry" is a hedge, not a decision**

- **Severity**: Blocker
- **Dimension**: Contrarian
- **Challenge/Risk**: Both conditions are circular. "Enter Wordsmith if the agent is multi-step" is true exactly if we build the agent to be multi-step — the condition gates our own todo list, not the world. "Enter HRT if we add Jev" is true exactly if we spend hours adding Jev. Neither condition has a checkpoint time, an owner, or a measurement that can fail. And they price the wrong thing: entering costs a checkbox; what costs hours is building to qualify. With ~15 clock hours and a web page that is literally `<main />`, these conditions will resolve by the clock, silently, in whatever direction the hours happened to flow — which is how hedges behave, not how decisions behave.
- **Alternative / Reuse Opportunity**: Convert each into a go/no-go with a time and a falsifiable trigger: "22:00 Saturday — if the competitor agent has produced ≥N verified, geocoded finds for the prepared startup, enter Wordsmith with its recorded trace; otherwise enter with whatever exists and stop." "HRT — enter only if the placement ranking already in scope is framed as budget-constrained selection; cost: zero hours." A condition that cannot fail is a wish, not a gate.

**3. Jev is YAGNI bought for a track title**

- **Severity**: Blocker
- **Dimension**: YAGNI & Code Minimization
- **Challenge/Risk**: Jev is real and does plug into Pydantic AI, so the description is accurate — but it appears nowhere in this repository except a hash string in `pnpm-lock.yaml`. Nothing discusses it, and its own documentation requires tuning confidence thresholds per question type against a pinned model version before the thresholds mean anything. Tuning needs a labelled corpus of competitor-campaign evidence, which needs the agent, which does not exist. The dependency chain is agent → corpus → tuning → track qualifier, inside one night, to gate a yes/no classification performed on perhaps dozens of snippets — a job a structured LLM output in the already-recorded stack does adequately for a demo. Worse, the question "is this article an outdoor campaign by X in New York" is negation- and implication-heavy, exactly what Jev's documentation warns it answers badly. And it still doesn't match HRT's stated themes (massive scale, diverse inputs, real-time ML); a tiny calibrated classifier is none of the three. New API key, new dependency, new tuning loop, one track, third priority.
- **Alternative / Reuse Opportunity**: The HRT-qualifying decision already exists in the plan for free. Ranking placements by cost per audience member and selecting the best set under the stated budget *is* data turning into an automated decision — that's the track title's second noun. The hourly MTA aggregate (dataset already checked, 47.4 million rows with hour and station) turned into a daypart recommendation is the first noun. Enter HRT by framing and charting in-scope code, not by adopting a model library.

**4. The "enables" legs rest on facts the repo contradicts or never checked**

- **Severity**: Major
- **Dimension**: Contrarian
- **Challenge/Risk**: "Published $8–20/day LinkNYC prices" appears nowhere in the repository, and the idea file records the opposite as an open problem: prices "probably unpublished," estimation method undecided. The only per-day figure recorded anywhere is adyoutiser's "from €2 a day," in the dropped idea file — a likely conflation. Same pattern in "which hours to buy": nothing verifies LinkNYC sells by hour at all. The strategy is strengthening its own "enables" argument with unrecorded facts. If a judge asks where $8–20 comes from and the answer is a shrug, the beat of the G-Research rubric that differentiates this project is the one that takes the hit.

- **Dimension**: Contrarian

What G-Research and Metaview score is the map, the gap layer, and the close from gap to buyable placements. The competition layer survives without a live agent: the plan already records a recorded-run fallback, and the agent's own design falls back to competitors' stores and offices, which is an API call, not browser work. The repo's own open problem says the agent may find few campaigns for small competitors. Declaring the most fragile, least-verifiable, highest-variance component inviolable — rather than the layer it feeds — is a Wordsmith-driven framing smuggled in as a "consequence."
- **Alternative / Reuse Opportunity**: Never-cut = the map with the gap layer and the placements close. The live agent is the *first* thing to convert to its recorded run plus OpenStreetMap points, not the last. That conversion is already a recorded decision; the strategy should be consistent with it.

A demo that also carries Wordsmith's complexity, HRT's prediction and a bank's cost-of-living angle in the same three minutes pleases none of them. Wordsmith's secondary criteria (tokens used, model, time to complete) punish a slow, sprawling agent — and complexity only scores if judges *perceive* it, so the recorded step trace is the scoring artefact, not the code. ---

**Summary for the orchestrator**: the strategy's real decision is not which tracks to enter — entry is free — but which hours to spend. The two structural fixes to carry back: make every condition a timed, falsifiable go/no-go, and make the never-cut pair the map and the placements close rather than the live agent.

Findings, in severity order. All file references are to the current tree; nothing has been modified.

---

**1. Severity: Blocker**
**Dimension: Conditional entries in a flat priority list**

**Structural risk:** The repository has no structure for a conditional track entry, and its own records argue against one. Entry is free: "we build one codebase and submit the same project to several sponsor tracks… there is no limit on how many tracks it can win" (root `AGENTS.md` line 7), and the ranking phase recorded the working rule "we submit one project and enter it into every sponsor track it fits" (`docs/idea-ranking.md` line 17). The priority list exists to order *effort* — "Prefer features that serve the priority tracks" (line 15) — not to gate entry. Of the two conditions in the proposal, the Wordsmith condition is already satisfied by the recorded design: the competitor agent is specified as multi-step and multi-site in `docs/ideas/audience-heatmap.md` line 21 (find competitors, search press, trade sites and social media, place each find) and line 66. The HRT conditions are the opposite: unmade decisions (the hourly view is "an open option, not a decision", line 25; the Jev model is recorded nowhere). So "conditional entry" is either a redundant restatement of the design or an unmade decision wearing an entry condition as a disguise. It also inverts the repo's own rule that "tracks decide what we build": if HRT is a priority track, the hourly view and decision model become build candidates *because* HRT calls for them, ranked by HRT's position — the entry doesn't wait on them.

**Recommendation:** Drop conditional syntax entirely. Enter every track that fits, as the recorded rule already says. Express the Wordsmith condition as what it already is: the recorded design of the agent, kept honest by the tracks-served annotations in `docs/status.md`. Express the HRT conditions as product decisions to be made on HRT's account, recorded in `docs/product.md` when and only when the user makes them, with HRT's third position governing how much time they get.

---

**2. Severity: Major**
**Dimension: Undefined term in a load-bearing condition**

**Structural risk:** "Jev" appears nowhere in this repository (the only match is a substring inside a lockfile integrity hash). A track position is being made conditional on integrating something no document in the repo defines, so no teammate reading the repo can check whether the condition is met — including a fresh session at 3am on Sunday. `docs/AGENTS.md` lines 7–8 forbid coined shorthand that cannot be searched for and require a term to be defined in half a sentence at first use. The "recorded Pydantic AI stack" half of the claim is fine: Pydantic AI in `tools/` is recorded in `docs/product.md` line 22. The Jev half is not.

**Recommendation:** If the user confirms the HRT position and the decision-model integration, the `product.md` decision line must define what the Jev decision model is and what it computes, in half a sentence, before anything depends on it. Until a definition exists, the HRT condition is uncheckable and should not be written anywhere as a condition.

---

**3. Severity: Major**
**Dimension: One decision, several files — half-written is the known failure mode**

**Structural risk:** The proposal records one consequence ("the agent and the map must not be cut") but a confirmed order makes statements false in more places than the TODO lines. Filling in "Priority tracks, most important first" falsifies "The track and challenge priorities above are still undecided" in the Project section of the root `AGENTS.md` (line 30) — exactly the fix-only-the-passage-you-read failure that `docs/AGENTS.md` lines 18–19 warn about. The challenges line (line 20) must be decided deliberately at the same time or left TODO on purpose, because the hourly view implies Tiger Data interest. `docs/pitch/judges/` does not exist yet, so "one file per track" is an entirely unbuilt obligation that confirmation activates. And the priorities themselves must not be copied into `docs/product.md`, whose own preamble (line 17) excludes them — while the consequential product decisions (hourly view, decision model, Bank of Scotland framing) belong only there.

**Recommendation:** Treat confirmation as one multi-file change with a write map (given in full below), and check every file in it in the same change. Root `AGENTS.md` is a shared-approval file, but the user's confirmation *is* the approval, so the agent can write it once confirmed.

---

**4. Severity: Major**
**Dimension: Stale statements the pivot already left behind**

**Structural risk:** The only substantive content in `docs/pitch/notes.md` (line 7, the placement-crowding answer) is built on the cut airport scope: Revolut on 300+ jet bridges, UK students' unions, sponsored newsletters. Those features were cut on 7 November 2026 (`docs/status.md` lines 9–10; superseded decision in `docs/product.md` line 29), and the current product's placement inventory is LinkNYC kiosks and bus shelters in New York. Under `docs/AGENTS.md` lines 18–19 these statements should have been corrected in place at the pivot and were not. This is independent of the track decision, but the Metaview polish target makes it worse: polish work will be planned from pitch notes that describe a product that no longer exists. The crowding *logic* (count the tool's own past recommendations as crowded) survives; the evidence is false.

**Recommendation:** Correct the answer in place now, replacing the airport and UK inventory with the recorded New York placement counts, before any Metaview-directed polish work starts.

---

**5. Severity: Major**
**Dimension: Priority order with no recorded reason**

**Structural risk:** The recorded analysis rates Wordsmith and HRT both moderate (`docs/ideas/audience-heatmap.md` lines 65–66), so the recorded ratings do not produce Wordsmith above HRT. The proposal simultaneously ranks HRT third and proposes the two things (hourly view, decision model) that the idea file itself says make HRT stronger. There is a coherent reason — Wordsmith is served by work already decided, HRT needs new work — but it exists nowhere in the repository. A priority list whose ordering rationale is unrecorded cannot do its job at crunch time, when the question "build the hourly view or harden the agent?" is exactly what the list exists to answer. The order does appear in `docs/status.md` line 11, but as an unordered annotation, not a ranking with reasons.

**Recommendation:** If the user confirms this order, record a short reason after each track name in the root `AGENTS.md` list, matching `product.md`'s decision-reason pattern (for example: Wordsmith second because the agent is already decided work; HRT third because it needs the hourly view and decision model to be competitive). Without that, the order is a bare assertion another session cannot re-derive or defend.

---

**6. Severity: Major**
**Dimension: Entering a track against its recorded fit**

**Structural risk:** The recorded analysis says "Bank of Scotland: weak. It serves startups, not consumers' cost of living" (`docs/ideas/audience-heatmap.md` line 67). Entering under a small-business reframing is allowed — the ranking doc is "a recommendation, not a decision" (line 3) and the root list is the decision home — but entering while the recorded analysis still says weak leaves a decision standing against an uncorrected record, which the correcting rules forbid. The reframing also carries a real judging risk the analysis must address: the brief says the tool helps "customers… make better decisions about their money and everyday lives" (`docs/event/tracks.md` line 48), and whether a bank judge reads "customers" as including small businesses spending a marketing budget is unverified. The governing analysis to correct is the idea file's own track-fit section, not `docs/track-groups.md`, whose Group A description concerns a personal-finance product this isn't.

**Recommendation:** Write the small-business reframing as track-fit reasoning first — cost, time, convenience and sustainability trade-offs in a small business's advertising spend — and, if the user accepts it, correct line 67 in place with that reasoning. If the user rejects the reframing, Bank of Scotland simply stays out of the list and no entry is lost, since a weak entry buys nothing the three real entries don't.

---

**7. Severity: Nit**
**Dimension: Challenge technology direction**

**Structural risk:** Direct answer to the rule question. Jev-for-HRT does not violate "challenges decide how, not what": Jev is not one of the seven MLH challenge technologies (`docs/event/challenges.md` lists Gemini, ElevenLabs, Entire, Solana, Tiger Data, Vultr, Auth0), and HRT is a sponsor track — strengthening a priority track with a decision model is the sanctioned direction. Hourly-view-for-Tiger-Data, as recorded, also does not violate: the idea file makes HRT the reason (line 65, "Stronger with the hourly view") and Tiger Data a conditional rider (line 73, "fits the hourly view if it is built"). The violation would appear in one specific future step: reviving the hourly view *because* Tiger Data wants time-series data, or adding Tiger Data's PostgreSQL extension to an architecture that currently computes results ahead of time in Python and serves them statically (`docs/product.md` lines 30–31). That extension is a live database service added for a challenge prize, which the rules permit only when it fits a feature the tracks already call for and costs no priority track.

**Recommendation:** Apply the test when the hourly view is decided: if it would be revived with Tiger Data absent, the reasoning is clean; if not, it isn't. If Tiger Data is then used and entered, it goes in the challenges TODO line, never the tracks list, and "sponsor tracks take priority over MLH challenges" (root `AGENTS.md` line 14) keeps the hourly view's justification resting on HRT alone.

---

**8. Severity: Nit**
**Dimension: A consequence already recorded in substance**

**Structural risk:** "The agent and the map must not be cut" proposes a new kind of hard rule, and the current document structure has no home for one. It is also already entailed: the map is the product itself (`docs/product.md` "What it is"), the agent is a recorded decision (line 26), and demo survival is covered by the recorded fallback run (line 32, and the idea file's Scope). What is *not* covered is descoping: if the agent is ever downgraded to mocked, the Wordsmith claim in `docs/status.md` line 11 becomes false and must be corrected there.

**Recommendation:** Don't create a new rule kind. The priority list itself, with per-track reasons (finding 5), is the record of this consequence; keep the tracks-served annotations in `status.md` honest and the protection is complete.

---

## Where a confirmed order must be written

Nothing below may be written until the user confirms; until then the TODO lines and the "still undecided" sentence are correct as they stand, and `docs/AGENTS.md` line 36 forbids recording unaccepted suggestions. The `pitch/notes.md` correction in item 6 is the one exception — the pivot already required it.

2. **`docs/product.md`**, Decisions, one line each, only for what the user separately confirms: the hourly view revival (reason: HRT); the Jev decision-model integration, defined at first use; the Bank of Scotland small-business framing; the Metaview polish bar as a demo-scope decision. The priority order itself must not go here.
3. **`docs/ideas/audience-heatmap.md`**, corrected in place: line 25's "open option, not a decision" once the hourly view is decided either way; line 67's weak Bank of Scotland rating if the reframing is accepted.
4. **`docs/status.md`**: hourly view and decision-model integration as Planned lines serving HRT; Bank of Scotland added to the gap map's served list only if entered.
5. **`docs/pitch/judges/`** (directory does not exist yet): one file per entered sponsor — `g-research.md`, `wordsmith.md`, `hrt.md`, plus `bank-of-scotland.md` only if entered. Metaview needs no file unless its judging turns out to require a separate submission; nothing recorded says it does (`docs/event/tracks.md` line 116).

7. **No change** to `docs/track-groups.md` or `docs/idea-ranking.md`: both self-declare as analysis and recommendation, and `docs/AGENTS.md` ties `track-groups.md` updates to changes in the event docs, not to our decisions.

## Objective
- Reframe the hackathon ad-placement product from airport rate-card hunting to estimating traffic/attention and producing heatmaps of effective places, then evaluate, review and plan the build.

## Requirements
- User asked to evaluate replacing niche price data with traffic estimation and heatmaps, covering both intra-city ("where in a city") and inter-city ("which cities") effectiveness.
- "it doesnt have to be uk it can be any city"; "which city or where to place in a city doesnt particularly matter either works, easiest / best choice wins".
